name: Djingili
confidence_why: Pensalfini's field description (1997 dissertation, 2003 reference grammar) gives a penultimate default with a large dictionary-listed class of initial- and antepenultimate-stressed words, Stanton 2015 repeats that reading, and the only differing statements are Chadwick 1975's older description of the plain penultimate default and Pensalfini 2000's comparative sketch that deliberately ignores the primary/secondary distinction, so the lexical reading has a clear winner but rests on a single modern fieldworker.
catalog_quote: Normal primary stress in items of more than one syllable is on the penultimate vowel. This applies also if the vowel is member of a diphthong. Secondary stress is normally on the vowel preceding the antepenultimate. (Chadwick 1975:9)
sweep_summary: Jingulu (djin1251, Mirndi) is in the catalog as OUT/lexical; the deciding quote shown is Chadwick 1975:9 (regular penultimate), but the compilers note (our earlier reading) already grounds the lexical exit on Pensalfini 2003:36-38 read at page-image grade. the list of works with stress in the title had one item, Pensalfini 2000 (ALS99), already held by the project and re-read: it is about Jingulu word stress (section 2.5, pp. 3-4) but is a foot-structure/suffix-coherence paper that idealises monomorphemic stress as initial-plus-alternating with primary/secondary ignored; its examples put primary stress on the rightmost non-final foot and show bárdarda initial-stressed, consistent with the 2003 grammar's lexical initial-stress class - it refines rather than decides the classification. New this search of works with stress in the title: the open MIT thesis Pensalfini 1997 (hdl 1721.1/10347, 60 MB PDF with text, saved) whose stress section pp. 70-78 is the first-hand original of the 2003 text and states the same penultimate-default-with-lexical-classes pattern plus 'the rightmost stressed element in a phonological word always bears primary stress' (p. 73); Pensalfini 2001 (PL 512, p. 396: main stress is the word's final stress, often on suffixes) and Stanton 2015 (fn. 1: 'stress is to some extent lexically specified') copied/re-read and both consistent. Chadwick 1975 has no open copy (print only, low priority since Pensalfini supersedes it). Nothing read contradicts the 'lexical' coding; the recommended deciding quote is Pensalfini 2003:36-38 (or 1997:70-72) rather than the Chadwick line. All files and URLs logged in

new_statements.quote: Words of two SBUs are stressed on the initial SBU. Words of three SBUs are generally stressed on the second SBU. Thus there is a general pattern of penultimate stress [p. 36] ... Among three-SBU words there are a large number of lexical exceptions which bear main stress on the initial SBU ... not so much an exception but a major lexical class [p. 37] ... Five-SBU words ... are almost evenly divided between words that have main stress on the penultimate SBU ... and words that have main stress on the antepenultimate SBU [p. 37] ... In summary, main stress always falls near the end of a word, but not on the final SBU [p. 38]

new_statements.reading: Right-edge, non-final main stress counted over vowels (SBUs), penultimate by default in 2-4 SBU words, but stress position at 3-6 SBUs is a dictionary-listed lexical property: a major initial-stress class at 3 SBUs, marked antepenult words at 4, an even penult/antepenult split at 5, antepenult preferred at 6, plus within-speaker free variation. Supports the catalog's 'lexical' out-code directly, whereas the catalog's quoted Chadwick 1975:9 line describes only the regular penultimate default.

audit.reasoning: The classification 'lexical' (not in the strict set, penult/antepenult window) rests on the modern reference grammar, Pensalfini 2003 (PL 536) sec. 2.3.1 pp. 36-38, which we hold in PDF and text; every quoted passage and both line locators were confirmed verbatim at the cited pages. The grammar states a penult default for 3- and 4-SBU words but a 'major lexical class' with initial stress among 3-SBU words, dictionary-marked antepenult 4-SBU words, an 'almost evenly divided' 5-SBU class with every word listed, antepenult preference at 6 SBUs, and word-level free variation -- i.e. main stress is confined to a non-final window but its position within it is learned per word, which is what the record codes; the StressTyp2 fixed: penultimate syllable coding follows the older Chadwick 1975 and is correctly flagged as contradicted. sources.citation: Pensalfini, Rob (2001). On the typological and genetic affiliation of Jingulu. In Simpson, Nash, Laughren, Austin & Alpher (eds), Forty years on: Ken Hale and Australian languages, 385-399. Pacific Linguistics 512.
sources.quote: Jingulu stress shows properties of neighbouring Pama-Nyungan languages within a non-Pama-Nyungan framework. Like the prefixing languages further to the north, the main stress in a Jingulu word is the final one. This means that main stress often falls on suffixes. However, with regard to suffix coherence (the degree to which suffixes resist being footed with material from other morphemes - see Pensalfini 1999c for discussion), Jingulu behaves more like Warlpiri than other languages.
sources.note: One-paragraph summary: the rightmost (final) stress of the word is primary, so main stress often lands on suffixes; suffix coherence is Warlpiri-like. Nothing on the lexical classes.

sources.citation: Pensalfini, Rob. 2000. Suffix coherence and stress in Australian languages. In John Henderson (ed.), Proceedings of the 1999 Conference of the Australian Linguistic Society. Perth: UWA (online proceedings), 10 pp.
sources.quote: Sec. 2 groups Jingulu with Pintupi, Diyari, Dyirbal, Warlpiri: 'stress on monomorphemic words: stress falls on the first syllable and on every second syllable thereafter, but never on the final syllable (the distinction between primary and secondary stress is ignored)'; fn. 1: Jingulu may treat the mora as the SBU (Pensalfini 1997). Sec. 2.5: Jingulu 'behaves like Warlpiri with respect to the boundary between root and suffix (a foot only contains nuclei from both root and suffix if a sequence of three unstressed syllables would otherwise result), but freely allows feet to contain nuclei from t
sources.note: Theoretical (OT) paper on suffix coherence in five Australian languages; Jingulu data from the author's own field notes (Pensalfini 1997). Idealises monomorphemic stress as left-aligned binary trochees (initial + every second syllable, never final) and explicitly ignores the primary/secondary distinction; Jingulu is Warlpiri-like at the root-suffix boundary (a root-final syllable is footed with a suffix only to avoid a three-syllable lapse) but freely lets a foot straddle two suffixes; a monosyllabic suffix is stressed only when not word-final.
